store.0: I'm a fourth-year computer science major, and I'm 21, almost 22. My schedule can get hectic with classes and projects, but my hobbies help me stay sane. I love coding, but I also enjoy other activities that give me a break and help me come back to programming with a fresh perspective.
store.1: Sailing is one of my favorite hobbies. It's unique among my friends, and I've been hooked since I was younger. I love the sense of freedom it gives me and the challenge of navigating the water and wind. It's a great way to clear my mind and enjoy the outdoors.
store.2: I'm a fourth-year Computer Science student, and I've seen how the culture has evolved over the years. I've discovered different communities that make this place feel like a second home. There are many ways to get involved beyond just coding in front of your laptop all day.
store.3: I joined the Computer Science Society, which hosts weekly meetups where we discuss new technologies, share personal projects, and have industry speakers. It's a welcoming environment for beginners. I can chat with fellow members who might have worked on similar topics in internships.

store.0: I'm a Computer Science major, and I'm in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is really packed, but it's a good kind of busy. I'm finally taking the higher-level courses that I've been looking forward to for a while. It's surreal to be at this stage, looking back on how far I've come. It feels like just yesterday I was in an intro class learning about simple data structures, and now I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even quantum computing basics. It's exciting to see how much I've grown and how much more I have to learn.
store.1: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm a huge fan of theory when it connects directly to real-world problem-solving. I find it fascinating to explore how we can optimize pathfinding in large networks or handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity. The class covers everything from dynamic programming approaches to approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems. It can be mind-bending at times, but in a good, challenging way. Our professor is great at explaining these complex concepts in an intuitive manner. She'll present a seemingly impossible problem on the board and then show us a strategy to approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my brain is buzzing with ideas and insights.
store.2: I'm also taking a Distributed Systems course(CS 2631), which is probably the second hardest. It's a lot of reading, group discussions, and we're working on a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure in itself. We have to collaborate with people who have different coding styles and sometimes different ideas about what the final product should look like. However, that's also the beauty of it. In a real-world setting, you're never working in a vacuum. You have to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle issues like concurrency and node failures. It can be nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a misplaced bracket in one of the config files. But once we fixed that and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment.
store.3: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward my major if I combine it with certain other classes. As a gamer at heart, this was a must-take for me. The professor is actually from the industry; he worked on a couple of indie games that got some decent traction. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, how to implement physics, and even a bit of user experience design. It's unbelievably fun because every assignment is super creative. Last time, I had to design a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, and it was all about balancing the difficulty curve so players wouldn't get frustrated and quit. Getting that design right was tricky, but it was also rewarding to see it come together.
store.4: I also have to mention my Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which I initially thought might be a bit intimidating. However, the professor's approach is to focus on conceptual understanding rather than just pure math. Of course, there is math involved, like linear algebra, but it's interspersed with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not actually building quantum computers, but we're modeling basic algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they theoretically outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing stuff and has made me rethink how I approach problems.
store.5: My Capstone Project course is definitely the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group and I decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It's a fancy-sounding project, but essentially, we're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts by analyzing tweets or posts for words that suggest a disaster or crisis. This project is pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major, including database management, building an API, front-end interface, and the ML pipeline. We're also learning about project management and how to keep ourselves organized. One person on our team is the designated "Scrum Master," so each week we have sprints, daily stand-ups, and all that agile jazz. It's a lot, but if we can pull it off, I'll be super proud.
store.6: I'm also taking a humanities elective called Philosophy of Mind, which is my last required non-CS elective. I chose it because it ties back into AI in interesting ways. We discuss topics like consciousness, the concept of mind, and how they might apply to artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have a lot of class discussions, which is a nice change of pace from all the coding in my other classes. It's great to take a step back and analyze abstract ideas. This class also helps me see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could one day mimic or simulate human thinking. Two weeks ago, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could ever truly experience qualia, such as the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and researching it was a fascinating experience. I believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, so I'm grateful for this perspective.
store.7: My schedule is pretty typical for a college student. Mondays and Wednesdays are the busiest days. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00 am. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are a bit lighter with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. Philosophy of Mind is on Thursday evenings, which can be tough if I'm tired from the rest of the day. Fridays are open, but I usually end up working on assignments, group projects, or labs. I also do some undergrad research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's interesting, but it definitely adds to the workload. I'm just trying to stay organized and make the most of my senior year.
store.8: The biggest challenge this semester is definitely balancing the group projects. The Capstone Project alone can consume around ten hours a week, and it can easily go up to more if we encounter any major bugs or if the model isn't training properly. Additionally, the Distributed Systems project is another significant time sink. My group tries to meet at least twice a week to discuss progress and coordinate our efforts. We also rely heavily on Slack or Discord to keep each other updated and share information. Coordinating five different people's schedules can be a mini-nightmare, but despite the stress, it's also exciting. This is one of my last chances to fully invest in a project that's purely academic and focused on learning, without the pressures of an actual job environment. It's a great opportunity to apply everything I've learned and make the most of my senior year.
store.9: I'm having a blast this semester! I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but now I've gotten better at problem-solving and time management. I still pull the occasional late night, but it's not as scary as it once was. Being a senior has given me a sense of confidence; I know that if I grind and keep my eye on the end goal, I'll eventually figure things out. The biggest takeaway is that after four years, you learn how to be resourceful, how to collaborate, and how to think critically. These classes are tough, no doubt, but they're also super rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building toward my future career, and that's a pretty great feeling.
store.10: I've been involved in undergraduate research since the end of my sophomore year, and it's been a fantastic experience. It's given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world, and I feel lucky to be a part of it. As a freshman, I didn't initially see myself going down the research route. I was more interested in coding projects and hackathons. However, one of my professors noticed my ability to combine technical coding with user experience and suggested I apply for a research assistant position in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific datasets. I was initially hesitant due to the perceived intimidation factor of research, but I decided to take the leap. It turned out to be a great decision.
store.11: I'm a fourth-year Computer Science student, and I've seen how the culture has evolved over the years. I've discovered different communities that make this place feel like a second home. There are many ways to get involved beyond just coding in front of your laptop all day.
store.12: I joined the Computer Science Society, which hosts weekly meetups where we discuss new technologies, share personal projects, and have industry speakers. It's a welcoming environment for beginners. I can chat with fellow members who might have worked on similar topics in internships.
store.13: I've been attending the VR/AR Club on and off since my sophomore year. I got hooked once I started doing research in immersive analytics, so it was natural for me to want to hang out with people who share that passion. The club is surprisingly hands-on—they have a VR lab in the engineering building with headsets, sensors, and quirky prototypes. We host demos where each person shows off their latest project, whether it's a mini-game or something more experimental like AR interfaces for everyday tasks. I just love the supportive vibe when people are genuinely excited about emerging tech.
store.14: I occasionally pop into the student-run radio station events, like their open-mic nights. It's a blast to see people sing, read poetry, or perform stand-up comedy. I remember one night, a friend from the Distributed Systems class performed an acoustic set. He's usually so quiet in class, but on stage, he was belting out these soulful tunes as if he was born for it. Moments like that remind me there's always more to someone than meets the eye when you're just coding together or doing group projects.
store.15: The campus has these iconic spots, like the central lawn where students hang out between classes. Student organizations set up booths there, and you can see fliers for various clubs. They often hand out freebies like stickers or candy to attract new members. My weakness is free pizza, so if a club includes that in their ad, I'm easily tempted. The lawn is also where big campus events like Tech Fest take place. During Tech Fest, project teams put up posters, do live demos of their prototypes, and recruiters look for innovative ideas. It's a big deal here, especially for engineering and CS folks.
store.16: I think campus culture is fairly collaborative. There are pockets of competition, especially among seniors trying to land top internships or job offers, but overall, people want to help each other succeed. I remember the campus hackathon in my second year, which was a huge eye-opener. Thousands of students from various backgrounds crammed into the student center for 24 or 36 hours straight, hacking away. It was chaotic but exhilarating. You'd see beginners learning the basics of GitHub while advanced teams used complex machine learning libraries to do real-time image recognition. Sponsors and mentors wandered around to see if anyone needed help. I formed a small team with a few casual acquaintances, none of us were super close friends. But the bond we formed during that all-nighter, eating stale pizza at 3 a.m., debugging code, and deliriously cheering each other on, was unlike anything I'd experienced before. That's the vibe I associate with campus life: you're all in the trenches together, forging friendships through these shared experiences and challenges.
store.17: Dorm life can be a huge part of campus culture. In my first two years, I stayed in a dorm specifically for engineering majors, which we jokingly called "The Engi-House." Late-night coding sessions in the common lounge were legendary. Someone would be working on an assignment for Data Structures, while another group might be streaming e-sports tournaments. The environment could get a bit intense at times, with stressed-out engineers fueled by energy drinks. However, it also meant that if you encountered a stumbling block, there was always someone nearby who could offer a quick pointer. Beyond academics, we'd hold potlucks, watch Netflix together, or even host a small talent show to blow off steam.
store.18: I've been volunteering at outreach events, particularly at the "Tech for Good" day organized by our CS department. Local high school students come to campus to learn about programming and problem-solving. I help run mini-workshops on topics like web development or basic Python. It's rewarding to see younger students light up when they create a simple game or animated webpage. I remember how I felt at that age, feeling overwhelmed by the tech world. Giving them a positive first experience is something I take pride in. Events like that show a different side of campus, beyond academic research and class assignments. It's about engaging with the community and inspiring the next generation to get excited about STEM fields.
store.19: We have a lively social scene beyond academics. Greek life is an option for those interested, but I never joined a fraternity. Instead, I found that specialized clubs are a great way to meet people with shared interests. For example, a friend who's into robotics joined the Robotics Team in his first semester and found a second family there. They now hang out on weekends, watch movies together, and grab dinner. I've also grown close to folks in the VR/AR Club and the CS Society. We don't just talk shop when we're together; we joke around, complain about cafeteria food, or plan weekend trips to the local hiking trails.
store.20: Senior Week is a staple of campus culture, and I'm about to experience it for the first time this year. It's a series of events leading up to graduation, including a formal dance, a carnival, and a day where seniors get pictures taken in their caps and gowns around iconic campus landmarks. I've heard it's bittersweet because it's the last hurrah before everyone scatters. My older pals who graduated last year said it was one of the best weeks of their college life, filled with laughter, nostalgia, and a bit of that sinking feeling that the journey's almost over. I'm both excited and a little anxious for it. I've been here for four years, made so many memories, and it's weird to think about not being a student anymore.
store.21: The Rivalry Game is a big campus tradition. Our sports teams face off against our biggest rival college in various sports. I'm not a dedicated sports fan, but I love the energy on campus that week. People deck themselves out in school colors, paint their faces, and parade around with banners. Sometimes, the night before the big football game, we have a massive pep rally with fireworks. It's a spectacle. Even if you don't go to the game itself, the vibe on campus is electric. Friends gather in dorm lounges or local bars to watch and cheer. If we win, the celebrations can last all weekend, and if we lose, we still find a way to commiserate together. It's a unifying moment for everyone, from business majors to art students to us nerdy engineers.
store.22: Our school's e-sports team has gained official recognition, and it's awesome to see a broader definition of competition and community. We now have an arena for e-sports, with a wide seating area and a big screen streaming the competitions live. During tournaments, you'll see a hundred or more students gathering to cheer on our team for League of Legends or Overwatch matches. It's great to see how e-sports has become a legitimate campus institution. I never would've guessed it would be this popular when I started college, but times are changing.
store.23: The "Midnight Breakfast" event during finals week is a huge morale booster. It's a small thing, but it reminds you that you're not alone in feeling anxious about final exams. Professors serve food, the school band might perform, and everyone takes a break from cramming. It's a great example of how campus culture ensures students have fun and camaraderie even during high-pressure times.
store.24: I think campus life here is what you make of it. If you're willing to explore, approach new people, and join clubs, you'll find a million ways to enrich your experience. It's easy to get lost in your workload, especially in a demanding major like Computer Science, but I've found that taking the time to attend events, volunteer, and connect with various communities has been incredibly rewarding. When I look back on my four years, I'll remember the late-night coding, sure—but I'll also remember the silly game nights in the dorm, the Tech Fest presentations, the hackathon adrenaline, and the excited cheers at the Rivalry Game. It's been a whirlwind, but I wouldn't trade it for anything. Let me know if you ever want a quick tour—I'd be happy to show you some of my favorite spots and introduce you to a few clubs. Honestly, there's something for everyone here, and I'm so glad I finally embraced all the campus has to offer.
